en: May my mind, distressed by the spreading rows of flames from the forest fire clinging to the vast wilderness of the sense-objects,
long become like a cakora bird fixed upon the moon-like face of Mukunda— the abode of all sweetness and the meeting place of abundant nectar. 1.
O support for the lotus-eyes of the daughter of the ocean!

With those eyes that delight the three worlds, which eclipse the pride of the heavy beauty of the rising morning lotuses, and which quickly cool me—me who am broken by the intensity of a fever surpassing a blazing fire—cool me at once! 2.

May some indescribable bank of clouds— remembered even in thought, dispelling the heat of youth through compassion for men with their unbroken physical splendor, encircled by hundreds of flashes of lightning,
clinging to the celestial trees on the banks of the Yamunā (the daughter of Mount Kalinda),
and kissing my mind— be present to me.

Constantly contemplating the forest interior on the banks of the Yamunā, the daughter of Mount Kalinda, [he] removes the burden of the exhaustion from the coming and going of living beings on the path;
surrounded by hundreds of creeping vines and endowed with a sweet luster, he is ever-present.
May the Tamāla tree quickly remove my excessive fatigue. ||4||

O Lord of the Yadus, I do not recall—even in my dreams—that instruction which you, with your stainless and nectar-sweet speech, gave to Nanda; for I was shameless, shrouded in the sense of "I" (egoism).
Yet, you still bear me, who am burdened by hundreds of such offenses, among your own kin. O Ocean of Mercy, there is no one more compassionate than you, nor anyone more intoxicated by pride than I.

Go to the netherworld, or depart for the city of the gods, or ascend to the peak of Mount Meru—if you desire your own welfare while buffeted by the succession of oceans—then, O friend, taste the elixir "Śrī Kṛṣṇa"; what is the use of other futile labors? 6.
Grapes have been tasted, sugar has been consumed in equal measure, abundant milk has been drunk,
nectar itself has been swallowed many times over, and the lip of Rambhā has been bitten—
tell me truly, O my life-breath, as you wander through this world again and again.
In some places, an outpouring of sweetness is perceived within the two syllables "Kṛṣṇa. (7)

The Vajra is the sovereign remedy for the mountains of evil, the perfected elixir for the manifestation of the Blessed One’s excellence, the rising orb of the fierce sun for the vast darkness of the night of false knowledge,
and the flame-haired fire for the cruel trees of the afflictions.
The two syllables "Kṛṣṇa" triumph as the gateway to the boat of liberation. ||8||
O mind, I tell you this for your own benefit: while grazing the herd of cows in Vṛndāvana, you must not form a bond with anyone who resembles a fresh rain-cloud.
For, by means of his gentle smiles that pour forth the nectar of beauty on all sides, he will utterly delude you and swiftly lead you, along with your beloved objects of sense, to destruction. 9.
She bestows an ineffable, supreme joy that plunges one into its depths; she is the shame within the throat that utterly dispels the mass of inner darkness.
She pours forth a sweetness esteemed even above grapes and other fruits— [May she protect you.]
O tongue, although you are a knower of flavors, tell me the name "Kṛṣṇa."
There are indeed many birds of beautiful form in this world, yet among them, my great longing is for the cātakas;
for by means of these witnesses, who remind one of their own friend, the cloud, there arises within the heart that indescribable Brahman known as Kṛṣṇa. 11.

He whose light illuminates the universe in all directions, and who is the objective support for the cognition "I am" even within all those who possess such knowledge—him, Viṣṇu, those who know the depths of their own hearts inquire about; O Śiva, Śiva! by whom can this logic of "otherness" and "non-otherness" among men be described? (12)
O friend, if you have a longing for service, then let the Lord of Lakṣmī be served;
if you have a desire for contemplation, then let the Wielder of the Discus be meditated upon;
if you long for conversation, then let the hymns of the Enemy of Smara be recited.
If you desire sleep for unimpeded happiness, let the mind sleep happily. 13.
Having forcibly and instantly uprooted the bond of non-discrimination— which is like a mass of intense heat from the summer of worldly existence that scorches the body—
one enters this pure lake of the nectar of the Self, cooled by the absence of desire.
The virtuous, having cast away the net of impurities, plunge into it. ||14||

Indeed, those who desire liberation from bondage perform sacrifices and other rituals; they devote themselves to extensive contemplation on the doctrines of hundreds of sages for the sake of inner peace;
and desiring to reach the further shore of the ocean of inauspiciousness, they bathe in sacred waters—all this is for men here who are subject to the delusion of worldly existence. ||15||
Having first kissed my feet, and then having embraced my calves, knees, thighs, navel, and heart, may my meditation sport upon the beauty of Viṣṇu’s lotus-face. 16.
O my life, though you see no means of crossing over, why do you languish?
Will the Son of Nanda not come at some point upon this path of the mind? 17.
May I not possess even for a moment wealth that is made beautiful by the sweet humming of swarms of bees wandering in intoxication over the temples of rutting elephants—
wealth which, for those submerged in it and whose eyes are agitated by the taste of riches,
causes the ease of service at the feet of Lord Hari to set. (18)
Why do you lie down so fearlessly? Death has arrived at the end of your life; or else, you may sleep in peace, for your mother, the Ganges, keeps watch nearby. (19)
Why do I torment my heart by running and running across the earth?
My supreme Lord, the son of Nanda, dwells eternally within my own prosperity. 20.
O mind, O mind, why do you incessantly bow at the two lotus feet of Him who destroys the afflictions of the heart,
yet cast me into the midst of the pit of worldly existence?
By this much alone, O son, your grief for your son will not depart.
Upon seeing the Lord of the Raghus from afar, the multitude of sages there fell into this doubt as to whether it was a mountain of emerald or a very young tamāla tree. (22)
"Could this be the daughter of the Sun? For she is not composed of water.

Or could it be the moonlight of emeralds? But how could that be so sweet?"—with such curiosity regarding the splendor of the Lord of the Raghus' body, by which people dwelling in the forest was he not first mistaken for these things? (23)
Immersed in doubt as to whether she was a fickle creeper fallen from a cloud or from a preeminent tree,
the wise monkey sighed deeply.
Thus he determined that she was a woman separated from her lover. ||24||
Prosperity resides in lowly homes, while in the dwellings of Brahmins there is only the clamor of poverty; alas, the wicked who tread the path of untruth enjoy a lifespan of a hundred years!
Seeing this injustice of yours, even though I am ablaze with the flaming crests of the fire of my wrath—
"O Lord of the Universe, what shall I do, since I have become a wretched one once again, O Lord of Bhavānī? ||25||
From the Jewel Mountain at its very base, encircled by the Malaya range, down to the shore of the ocean—let all those who are skilled in composing poetry speak without hesitation!
Who else besides me is fortunate enough to occupy the position of a master over words that possess the fortune of a sweetness like the smooth stream of juice flowing from the heart of a grape? (26)
The Goddess of Speech, who pays no heed to the sound of lute strings, drinks the nectar-like essence of his words;
hearing that speech so pleasing to the ear, either the king of scholars shakes his head, or this is merely Paśupati, the beast-king. (27)
Do not cast away my words with indifference,
for they shall display many playful graces upon the mouths of those bees who delight in the nectar of the lotus of poetry— those companions of the wicked whose minds are submerged in envy. (28)
Honey, grapes, nectar itself, or even the ambrosia of beautiful lips—
surely these do not fail to bring joy to some people at one time or another. Alas, those whose minds are so dull that they find no delight in these are surely dead, even while living.
The speech of the Lord of the World generates joy in others. ||29||

O friend, if you are truly skilled in composition—your speech being exalted by the abandonment of pride through a sweetness like that of honey-ripened grapes—then speak your poem freely in the presence of those such as me;
otherwise, do not let it remain within your heart like a misdeed committed by yourself that has been kept secret. (30)
Even compared to the supreme sweetness of grapes, milk, sugarcane, honey, and nectar, this sweetness of the poetry of Paṇḍitarāja alone is worthy of praise. (31)
The scriptures have been mastered, all daily rites have been performed,
and my youth has been spent at the palm-like hand of the beloved of Delhi;
now, with all latent desires abandoned, I serve Lord Hari in the midst of Mathurā.
All this was composed by Sarvapaṇḍitarājarājatilaka, surpassing the world. ||32||
Fearing that those of wicked conduct born of paramours might steal them, I have made this casket for my jewel-like verses. 33.
Enveloping the web of the world with the fresh nectar of his moonlight, instantly quelling the threefold suffering of all people,
he has taken refuge in the forest of Vṛndāvana, surrounded by the entire host of gods who bow before him.
May this new rain-cloud dispel the darkness within my heart. ||34||

May the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis remove my agony, as a rain-cloud does for one whose body is scorched by the spreading, terrifying flames of the fierce solar orb in summer—just as a cloud in the monsoon season does. 35.
In this shoreless saṃsāra, a path through the forest of treacherous poisons, I, dull-witted, have wandered again and again without finding rest; for me,
thus utterly exhausted, here is the refuge on the bank of the daughter of the sun.
May the young Tamāla tree of Hari dispel the heat on all sides. ||36||
May he who was sportively embraced by the Daughter of the Ocean,
like a tamāla tree entwined by a priyaṅgu creeper,
dwell within my heart at the time of the end of my life.
May the Blessed Lord, whose navel is like a lotus, be victorious! ||37||
May some indescribable bank of clouds, capable of swelling the mass of joy in my eyes, quickly dispel my anguish. 38.
O embodiment of compassion, by whom even Gaṇikā, Jāmbila, and others were rescued, surely I too, sinking in the desert pit of worldly existence, must not be entirely neglected by you. (39)

May my state of non-differentiation from the Supreme Self arise, [viewing] the Malaya breeze and the Kalakuta poison as one, the tresses of a beautiful woman and the coils of a serpent as one, and the Chandala and the Self-born Brahma as one. 40.
The entire world is indeed perishable, and within it, the body is especially so;
alas, how much labor do people expend for its sake! 41.
Alas! Even though one perceives every living being entering the jaws of death at every moment, why does the mind still not turn away from sense objects even today? 42.
Let the fortune of sovereignty perish this very instant, or let the edges of swords fall upon me;
let Death seize my head by force, but my mind shall not depart even slightly from righteousness.
Let my enemy blow a dense mass of fire incessantly upon my head, or let him strike me with the edge of a sword;
I shall not say even a single word, however minute.
Thus ends the *Śāntivilāsa*, composed by the illustrious scholar Jagannātha Paṇḍita.
